paragraphs.text: Grading Policies for Introduction to Literature
Grading Scale
Essays (60%)
Your four major essays will combine to form the main part of the grade for this course: Essay 1＝10%; Essay 2＝15%; Essay 3＝15%; Essay 4＝20%.
Group Assignments (30%)

Students will work in groups to complete four assignments (作业) during the course. All the assignments will be submitted by the assigned date through Blackboard, our online learning and course management system.
Daily Work/In-Class Writings and Tests/Group Work/Homework (10%)

Class activities will vary from day to day, but students must be ready to complete short in-class writings or tests drawn directly from assigned readings or notes from the previous class’ lecture/discussion, so it is important to take careful notes during class. Additionally, from time to time I will assign group work to be completed in class or short assignments to be completed at home, both of which will be graded.
Late Work

An essay not submitted in class on the due date will lose a letter grade for each class period it is late. If it is not turned in by the 4th day after the due date, it will earn a zero. Daily assignments not completed during class will get a zero. Short writings missed as a result of an excused absence will be accepted.

Like most of us, I try to be mindful of food that goes to waste. The arugula (芝麻菜) was to make a nice green salad, rounding out a roast chicken dinner. But I ended up working late. Then friends called with a dinner invitation. I stuck the chicken in the freezer. But as days passed, the arugula went bad. Even worse, I had unthinkingly bought way too much; I could have made six salads with what I threw out.

In a world where nearly 800 million people a year go hungry, “food waste goes against the moral grain,” as Elizabeth Royte writes in this month’s cover story. It’s jaw-dropping how much perfectly good food is thrown away—from “ugly” (but quite eatable) vegetables rejected by grocers to large amounts of uneaten dishes thrown into restaurant garbage cans.

Producing food that no one eats wastes the water, fuel, and other resources used to grow it. That makes food waste an environmental problem. In fact, Royte writes, “if food waste were a country, it would be the third largest producer of greenhouse gases in the world.”

If that’s hard to understand, let’s keep it as simple as the arugula at the back of my refrigerator. Mike Curtin sees my arugula story all the time—but for him, it’s more like 12 boxes of donated strawberries nearing their last days. Curtin is CEO of DC Central Kitchen in Washington, D. C., which recovers food and turns it into healthy meals. Last year it recovered more than 807,500 pounds of food by taking donations and collecting blemished (有瑕疵的) produce that otherwise would have rotted in fields. And the strawberries? Volunteers will wash, cut, and freeze or dry them for use in meals down the road.

Such methods seem obvious, yet so often we just don’t think. “Everyone can play a part in reducing waste, whether by not purchasing more food than necessary in your weekly shopping or by asking restaurants to not include the side dish you won’t eat,” Curtin says.
The elderly residents (居民) in care homes in London are being given hens to look after to stop them feeling lonely.

The project was dreamed up by a local charity (慈善组织) to reduce loneliness and improve elderly people’s wellbeing. It is also being used to help patients suffering dementia, a serious illness of the mind. Staff in care homes have reported a reduction in the use of medicine where hens are in use.
Among those taking part in the project is 80-year-old Ruth Xavier. She said: “I used to keep hens when I was younger and had to prepare their breakfast each morning before I went to school.”
“I like the project a lot. I am down there in my wheelchair in the morning letting the hens out and down there again at night to see they’ve gone to bed.”

“It’s good to have a different focus. People have been bringing their children in to see the hens and residents come and sit outside to watch them. I’m enjoying the creative activities, and it feels great to have done something useful.”
There are now 700 elderly people looking after hens in 20 care homes in the North East, and the charity has been given financial support to roll it out countrywide.

Wendy Wilson, extra care manager at 60 Penfold Street, one of the first to embark on the project, said: “Residents really welcome the idea of the project and the creative sessions. We are looking forward to the benefits and fun the project can bring to people here.”
Lynn Lewis, director of Notting Hill Pathways, said: “We are happy to be taking part in the project. It will really help connect our residents through a shared interest and creative activities.”

Human speech contains more than 2,000 different sounds, from the common “m” and “a” to the rare clicks of some southern African languages. But why are certain sounds more common than others? A ground-breaking, five-year study shows that diet-related changes in human bite led to new speech sounds that are now found in half the world’s languages.

More than 30 years ago, the scholar Charles Hockett noted that speech sounds called labiodentals, such as “f” and “v”, were more common in the languages of societies that ate softer foods. Now a team of researchers led by Damián Blasi at the University of Zurich, Switzerland, has found how and why this trend arose.

They discovered that the upper and lower front teeth of ancient human adults were aligned (对齐) , making it hard to produce labiodentals, which are formed by touching the lower lip to the upper teeth. Later, our jaws changed to an overbite structure (结构) , making it easier to produce such sounds.

The team showed that this change in bite was connected with the development of agriculture in the Neolithic period. Food became easier to chew at this point. The jawbone didn’t have to do as much work and so didn’t grow to be so large.

Analyses of a language database also confirmed that there was a global change in the sound of world languages after the Neolithic age, with the use of “f” and “v” increasing remarkably during the last few thousand years. These sounds are still not found in the languages of many hunter-gatherer people today.

This research overturns the popular view that all human speech sounds were present when human beings evolved around 300,000 years ago. “The set of speech sounds we use has not necessarily remained stable since the appearance of human beings, but rather the huge variety of speech sounds that we find today is the product of a complex interplay of things like biological change and cultural evolution,” said Steven Moran, a member of the research team.

It was the day of the big cross-country run. Students from seven different primary schools in and around the small town were warming up and walking the route (路线) through thick evergreen forest.

I looked around and finally spotted David, who was standing by himself off to the side by a fence. He was small for ten years old. His usual big toothy smile was absent today. I walked over and asked him why he wasn’t with the other children. He hesitated and then said he had decided not to run.
What was wrong? He had worked so hard for this event!

I quickly searched the crowd for the school’s coach and asked him what had happened. “I was afraid that kids from other schools would laugh at him,” he explained uncomfortably. “I gave him the choice to run or not, and let him decide.”

I bit back my frustration (懊恼) . I knew the coach meant well—he thought he was doing the right thing. After making sure that David could run if he wanted, I turned to find him coming towards me, his small body rocking from side to side as he swung his feet forward.

David had a brain disease which prevented him from walking or running like other children, but at school his classmates thought of him as a regular kid. He always participated to the best of his ability in whatever they were doing. That was why none of the children thought it unusual that David had decided to join the cross-country team. It just took him longer—that’s all. David had not missed a single practice, and although he always finished his run long after the other children, he did always finish. As a special education teacher at the school, I was familiar with the challenges David faced and was proud of his strong determination.

paragraphs.function: 给出迟交作业的具体扣分与处理规则。

group-2022-i-reading-b.overview: 本文是一篇关于食物浪费（food waste）的议论性随笔。作者以自己丢弃芝麻菜的小故事开篇，引出食物浪费普遍且常常是无意识发生的现象，进而指出食物浪费的环境危害，最后通过 DC Central Kitchen 的 Mike Curtin 给出回收食物、减少浪费的解决方案与建议。

discourseStructure.summary: 由个人轶事切入（现象）→ 揭示食物浪费的普遍性与道德问题 → 论证其环境危害（因果）→ 用 Curtin 的实践给出解决方案 → 以 Curtin 的建议收尾，号召人人参与。

paragraphs.summary: 作者讲述自己本想用芝麻菜做沙拉，却因加班、赴约而把它放坏，并坦言当初买得太多。
paragraphs.function: 以个人轶事开篇，引出主题，说明食物浪费常在不经意间发生。

paragraphs.summary: 引用 Elizabeth Royte 的话，指出在近 8 亿人挨饿的世界里食物浪费有违道德，且数量惊人。
paragraphs.function: 提升到社会与道德层面，指出食物浪费的普遍性与严重性。

paragraphs.summary: 指出生产没人吃的食物浪费了水、燃料等资源，使食物浪费成为环境问题，并引用其为全球第三大温室气体排放源的说法。
paragraphs.function: 论证食物浪费的环境危害，构成因果论证。

paragraphs.summary: 介绍 Mike Curtin 与他任 CEO 的 DC Central Kitchen，该机构回收食物并将其制成健康餐食，去年回收超 807,500 磅食物。
paragraphs.function: 用具体实践案例提供解决方案。

paragraphs.summary: Curtin 指出人人都能出一份力，比如每周购物不买超量、请餐厅不上自己不吃的配菜。
paragraphs.function: 以建议收尾，号召读者从日常行为减少浪费。

group-2022-i-reading-c.overview: 本文是一篇新闻报道，介绍伦敦养老院让老人照看母鸡以减少孤独感、改善身心健康的公益项目，并通过参与者和项目负责人的话展示项目效果与推广前景。

discourseStructure.summary: 全文先点明项目核心做法，再说明项目缘起与目的，接着以老人 Ruth Xavier 的亲身感受作为例证，随后给出项目规模与推广情况，最后引用两位项目负责人的话表明各方对项目的欢迎态度。

paragraphs.summary: 伦敦养老院里的老年居民被分配照看母鸡，以缓解他们的孤独感。
paragraphs.function: 开篇点题，概括项目的核心做法与目的。

paragraphs.summary: 项目由当地慈善组织发起，旨在减少孤独、改善老人福祉，还用于帮助痴呆症患者，且养老院报告用药量减少。
paragraphs.function: 说明项目的发起方、目的及初步成效。

paragraphs.summary: 80岁的 Ruth Xavier 参与项目，她回忆年轻时也养过鸡，上学前要先喂鸡。
paragraphs.function: 引入具体参与者作为例证，建立其与养鸡的渊源。

paragraphs.summary: Ruth 很喜欢这个项目，早晚都坐着轮椅去放鸡、看鸡归笼。
paragraphs.function: 展示参与者对项目的喜爱及日常参与。

paragraphs.summary: Ruth 认为有了不同的关注点很好，孩子和居民都来看鸡，她享受创造性活动，觉得做了有用的事很棒。
paragraphs.function: 进一步表现参与者获得的成就感与积极心理体验。

paragraphs.summary: 目前东北部20家养老院已有700位老人照看母鸡，慈善组织获得资金支持以在全国推广。
paragraphs.function: 说明项目规模及向全国推广的进展。

paragraphs.summary: 项目最早参与地之一的护理经理 Wendy Wilson 表示居民欢迎该项目和创意活动，并期待项目带来的好处与乐趣。
paragraphs.function: 引用项目方人物的话，表明居民欢迎与积极期待。

paragraphs.summary: Notting Hill Pathways 主管 Lynn Lewis 表示乐于参与，认为项目能通过共同兴趣和创意活动把居民联系起来。
paragraphs.function: 引用另一位负责人的话，进一步强化各方对项目的欢迎态度。

group-2022-i-reading-d.overview: 本文是一篇科普说明文，介绍了苏黎世大学 Damián Blasi 团队的一项五年研究：饮食变化导致人类咬合方式改变，进而产生了如“f”“v”这类唇齿音，这些新音如今出现在世界半数语言中。

discourseStructure.summary: 文章先提出问题（为何某些语音更常见），再引出研究发现；接着从牙齿对齐到覆咬合的解剖变化、与新石器时代农业发展的关联、语言数据库的佐证逐层展开，最后用研究者的话总结研究意义。

paragraphs.summary: 人类语音有两千多种声音，但某些声音更常见；一项五年研究表明饮食导致的咬合变化产生了新的语音。
paragraphs.function: 提出问题并引出研究核心发现，作为全文引子。

paragraphs.summary: 回顾 Hockett 三十多年前的观察：吃软食社会的语言中唇齿音更常见；Blasi 团队进一步研究其成因。
paragraphs.function: 交代研究背景，承接前文并引出研究焦点。

paragraphs.summary: 古人类上下门牙对齐，难以发唇齿音；后来颌部变为覆咬合结构，使发音更容易。
paragraphs.function: 从解剖角度解释唇齿音难易变化的机制。

paragraphs.summary: 咬合变化与新石器时代农业发展相关：食物更易咀嚼，颌骨工作量减少，因而不再长得很大。
paragraphs.function: 解释咬合结构变化的深层原因（农业与饮食）。

paragraphs.summary: 语言数据库分析也证实新石器时代后世界语言声音发生全球性变化，“f”“v”使用显著增加，而许多狩猎采集民族语言中仍没有这些音。
paragraphs.function: 用语言数据库分析为研究结论提供佐证。

paragraphs.summary: 该研究推翻了人类所有语音在约三十万年前进化时就已存在的流行观点；研究者 Steven Moran 指出语音是生物变化与文化演化复杂相互作用的产物。
paragraphs.function: 总结研究意义并引用研究者观点收束全文。

q-2022-i-032.questionFocus: 考查 Damián Blasi 的研究聚焦于人类语音的哪个方面，需定位研究内容。

trap.sourceQuote: the huge variety of speech sounds that we find today is the product of a complex interplay of things like biological change and cultural evolution
trap.sourceEntity: the huge variety of speech sounds
trap.explanation: “variety（多样性）”出自文末 Moran 对语音总体的概括，而非 Blasi 研究所聚焦的对象；Blasi 团队研究的是新语音如何随咬合变化而发展，二者对象不符。

trapEvidence.quote: the huge variety of speech sounds that we find today is the product of a complex interplay of things like biological change and cultural evolution

q-2022-i-033.questionFocus: 考查古人类成人难以发唇齿音的原因，需定位第三段的解剖学描述。
q-2022-i-033.stemTranslationZh: 为什么古代人类成人难以发出唇齿音？

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.optionTranslationZh: 他们的上门牙比下门牙少。

trap.claim: 古人类上门牙比下门牙少。
trap.explanation: 原文只说上下门牙“aligned（对齐）”，从未提及上下门牙数量多少之别，属无中生有。

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.optionTranslationZh: 他们不能轻松地张开和闭合嘴唇。

trap.claim: 古人类不能轻松张合嘴唇。
trap.explanation: 原文将唇齿音难发归因于牙齿对齐的咬合结构，从未提及嘴唇张合困难，属无中生有。

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.optionTranslationZh: 他们的颌部结构不便（于发这种音）。

evidence.quote: the upper and lower front teeth of ancient human adults were aligned (对齐) , making it hard to produce labiodentals
evidence.anchor: 门牙对齐导致难发唇齿音

evidence.quote: Later, our jaws changed to an overbite structure (结构) , making it easier to produce such sounds.
